html:
Portuguese Angola was Portugal's colony on the Atlantic coast of southern Africa, from 1575 until independence as Angola in 1975. The map shows it under this name in 1880, 1938 and 1945.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda in 1576. For three centuries Portuguese rule rarely reached far inland. The colony's business was the slave trade: wars against Ndongo and its queen Nzinga, and trade with inland states, sent millions of captives across the Atlantic, above all to Brazil. The Dutch held Luanda from 1641 to 1648, until a fleet from Brazil retook it.

After the Berlin Conference of 1884 Portugal had to prove it controlled the interior, and it fought a long series of campaigns, not finished until the 1920s. Under the Estado Novo dictatorship from the 1930s, white settlers poured in, Africans were forced to work or grow cash crops, and coffee and diamonds made the colony one of Portugal's most valuable. In 1951 it was renamed an overseas province. The war of independence began in 1961.
